sections.h2: Where is Naugatuck and how is it governed?
sections.html:
Naugatuck is a consolidated borough and town in New Haven County, Connecticut, just south of Waterbury along the Naugatuck River. It belongs to the Naugatuck Valley Planning Region and covers 16.39 square miles.

The borough is the only consolidated town and borough in the state. Every other Connecticut borough is a special-services district inside a town. For a seller, the practical effect is that Naugatuck keeps both a town clerk and a borough clerk handling official records, so it helps to ask your closing attorney which office holds a given document.

The community includes several named sections. Union City sits on the east side of the river, Straitsville lies to the southeast along Route 63, and Millville runs along Rubber Avenue on the west side. Buyers and agents often use those names, so a cash buyer who knows them can place a house quickly.

sections.h2: What shaped Naugatuck's housing and neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Rubber manufacturing shaped the borough. Settlement began as early as 1702, the area was known as Salem Bridge until the town took its current name, and Naugatuck incorporated in 1844 from parts of Waterbury, Bethany and Oxford. In 1892 nine firms combined to form the United States Rubber Company, later Uniroyal, which was organized in Naugatuck.

The factory story did not stop there. U.S. Rubber introduced Naugahyde in 1936, the Risdon company made metal closures and cosmetic packaging, and the Peter Paul candy plant, maker of Mounds and Almond Joy, closed in 2007. Many sellers here own a house in a neighborhood that grew up around mills that no longer operate, which can mean older construction and deferred repairs.

Water has also left a mark. On August 19, 1955, the Naugatuck River flooded after more than 10 inches of rain from Hurricane Diane, and the flood reshaped the borough's riverfront. If your house is near the river or a brook, ask your insurer and your attorney about flood zone status before you list, since a buyer's lender will ask the same question.

sections.h2: How do Naugatuck property taxes work when you sell?
sections.html:
Naugatuck real estate taxes are billed in two installments, due July 1 and January 1. The tax office states that for the July 1, 2026 installment, bills were mailed by June 24, 2026 and the last day to pay without interest was August 3, 2026. The second half is due January 1, 2027 and is not late if paid by February 1, 2027.

The tax office notes that no second bill is sent. The top of the bill is the January amount and the bottom is the July amount, so keep the original. Late payments accrue interest at 1.5 percent per month, and a partial month counts as a full month, so an installment paid in August is charged 3 percent.

  • Mill rate for the 2025 grand list: 40.44 for real estate and personal property.
  • One mill is one dollar of tax per $1,000 of assessed value, so an assessed value of $100,000 at 40.44 mills works out to $4,044 a year.
  • Past-due statements for real estate go out in September and again in February, before lien continuing certificates are filed in June.
  • The tax office is at 229 Church Street and the lobby in Town Hall is open Monday to Thursday 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and Friday 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m.

Unpaid installments, interest and liens are normally settled from sale proceeds at the closing table. Ask the tax office for a current balance before you set a closing date, because the figure changes each month.

sections.h2: What does the Connecticut conveyance tax cost on a Naugatuck sale?
sections.html:
Connecticut charges a conveyance tax on the deed whenever the consideration is $2,000 or more, and the town clerk will not record the deed until the return is filed and the tax is paid. On residential property it has a state part and a municipal part.

  • State part: 0.75 percent of the price up to $800,000, 1.25 percent from $800,000.01 to $2,500,000, and 2.25 percent above $2,500,000.
  • Municipal part: one-fourth of one percent of the price, which goes to the municipality where the deed is recorded.
  • Non-residential property other than unimproved land is charged the state part at 1.25 percent.
  • A sale of a principal residence with a foundation made from defective concrete containing pyrrhotite can be exempt if a licensed engineer certifies it, and only for the first sale after certification.

The statute also lets a targeted investment community add up to another quarter of one percent. Your purchase contract and closing attorney decide who pays the tax on your sale.

sections.h2: How do roads, rail and schools affect selling in Naugatuck?
sections.html:
Naugatuck is reachable by highway and by train. The Route 8 expressway runs to Waterbury, Derby, Torrington and Bridgeport, Route 63 heads to New Haven, and Route 68 goes toward Durham. The Naugatuck station serves the Waterbury Branch of the New Haven Line.

The public schools run in four elementary schools for grades K to 4, two intermediate schools for grades 5 and 6, one middle school for grades 7 and 8, and Naugatuck High School for grades 9 to 12. The high school had an $81 million renovation that began in 2013 and finished by fall 2015, and its current enrollment is 1,267.

The borough also has a National Register listing for the Naugatuck Center Historic District, among other sites. If you own a house near the Green or on Church Street, ask the borough whether any local review applies before you start repairs.

sections.h2: Which ways of selling a Naugatuck house are available?
sections.html:
Most Naugatuck owners choose between three routes: list with an agent, sell on their own, or take a cash offer from a company that buys as-is. Each trades time, cost and certainty differently.

  • Listing with an agent can reach the widest group of buyers, but it usually means showings, buyer financing, appraisal and repair requests.
  • Selling on your own saves a commission and adds paperwork, marketing and negotiation to your list.
  • A cash sale to a buyer like us skips lender approval and the repair list, and you choose the closing date within what the title work allows.

A cash offer reflects the condition of the house, so it can differ from a retail listing price. We do not promise a number before we review the property, and you can say no to an offer without owing anything.

sections.h2: What do Naugatuck sellers usually run into?
sections.html:
Common situations in a former mill borough involve age, inheritance and timing. A house that has sat with deferred maintenance can be hard to finance, since a lender's appraiser may flag roof, foundation, heating or electrical problems.

Inherited houses add a second layer. Heirs may live out of state, the title may still be in a parent's name, and the estate may need court steps before anyone can sign a deed. Back taxes matter too, because the tax office adds interest each month and files lien continuing certificates in June after its past-due notices.

Tenant-occupied houses, code questions and a mortgage that is behind round out the list. In each case, a short call with a title company or attorney can show what has to be cleared before closing.

sections.h2: What are the steps to sell a Naugatuck house for cash?
sections.html:
1. Share the address, condition and your timeline with us.
  2. We review the house and any liens, taxes or title issues.
  3. You receive a written offer and decide at your own pace.
  4. If you accept, a title company or attorney opens the file and orders the title search.
  5. The conveyance tax return is filed with the town clerk, back taxes are paid from proceeds, and the deed is recorded.

The Naugatuck tax office can give you a payoff figure, and the town clerk can confirm recording requirements. We are not a law firm, so confirm legal and tax questions with a Connecticut attorney or the official office.

faqs.q: How much is the Naugatuck mill rate?
faqs.a: The tax office lists a mill rate of 40.44 for real estate and personal property on the 2025 grand list, and 32.46 for motor vehicles. Ask the office for the current figure before you estimate a payoff.

faqs.q: When are Naugatuck property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate taxes are due in two installments, July 1 and January 1. The office says the July 2026 installment was not late until after August 3, 2026, and the January 1, 2027 installment is not late if paid by February 1, 2027.

faqs.q: What interest does Naugatuck charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: The tax office charges 1.5 percent per month on late payments, and a partial month counts as a whole month. An installment paid in August is charged 3 percent.

faqs.q: Do I pay the Connecticut conveyance tax when I sell in Naugatuck?
faqs.a: The tax is imposed on the deed, and the contract and your closing attorney decide who pays it. On residential property under $800,000 the combined state and municipal rate is 1 percent, made up of 0.75 percent state and 0.25 percent municipal.

faqs.q: Is there a flood risk to consider in Naugatuck?
faqs.a: Naugatuck flooded on August 19, 1955, after more than 10 inches of rain from Hurricane Diane. Ask your insurer and attorney about the flood status of your specific lot.

faqs.q: Which Naugatuck office records the deed?
faqs.a: Naugatuck has both a town clerk and a borough clerk. Ask your closing attorney or the town clerk which office takes the deed and conveyance tax return.
